title: AT&T Is in Trump’s Portfolio. Buy Before Earnings?
detail:
AT&T Is in Trump’s Portfolio. Buy Before Earnings?
Fahad Saleem
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 5:20 AM MST 3 min read
T
Trade AT&T on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T) is down about 10% over the past year. It is one of the top stock picks in President Donald Trump's latest stock portfolio. Let's see whether the stock can rebound.

Bull Case

AT&T keeps customers longer when they bundle its fiber internet with its wireless service, and 42.5% of its advanced home internet customers already take both. Management says these customers stay longer and spend more, and it targets a 50% rate. The company plans to reach more than 60 million fiber locations by 2030. Its purchase of Lumen's consumer fiber business added more than 4 million locations where only about 25% of homes are customers, against about 40% in AT&T's own footprint. Management explained why bundled customers stay longer on its first-quarter earnings call. Click to read the call transcript here. AT&T is also retiring its copper network to cut costs and raised its 2026 buyback plan.

Bear Case

AT&T spends heavily to build fiber, and its debt is rising. After the EchoStar spectrum purchase, management expects leverage to climb from 2.68 times EBITDA to about 3.2 times before it falls back. Satellite companies are the larger worry, and they explain much of the drop in the stock. SpaceX and Amazon's Leo are pushing into broadband and mobile service, and Oppenheimer downgraded AT&T in June, saying satellite broadband puts its subscriber growth at risk. Carillon Eagle Growth & Income Fund said in its investor letter that AT&T lagged because investors fear a new competitor. Click to read their reasons here. Higher interest rates also make the dividend less attractive and raise debt costs, and AT&T has held its quarterly dividend flat since 2022.

Valuation

AT&T trades at a forward P/E of 10.02, below the sector median of 12.75 and the market's 19.1, and just above its own five-year average of 9.19. Analyst consensus has earnings per share growing 10.31% in 2026 and 9.92% in 2027, close to the market's long-run rate of about 10%. Revenue is forecast to grow only 2.83% and 2.23%, so cost cuts, lower depreciation and buybacks drive the earnings growth. Management guides to double-digit adjusted EPS growth through 2028. Growth slows in the fourth quarter, with analysts expecting just 1.58%, partly because interest costs rise after the EchoStar deal. Buyers at this price are betting that earnings keep growing near 10% a year while revenue grows 2% to 3%. If cost savings stall or competition forces price cuts, growth falls toward revenue growth and a multiple near 10 looks fair.

title: JPMorgan sees 67% upside in a hidden SpaceX bet
detail:
JPMorgan sees 67% upside in a hidden SpaceX bet
Faizan Farooque, Celine Provini
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 7:17 PM MST 6 min read
ECHO
SPCX
T
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

EchoStar (ECHO) used to be an awkward mix of satellite television, wireless ambitions, spectrum holdings, and a heavy debt load.

Investors should now see it differently, according to JPMorgan.

Reversing the firm's prior Underweight position, analyst Sebastiano Petti began covering EchoStar as Overweight and set a price objective of $144. That implies roughly 67% upside from where the shares traded when the call was published, according to MarketWatch.

The cause is not an abrupt change at Hughes or Dish.

SpaceX is the company.

EchoStar sold $20 billion in spectrum to SpaceX and multibillion-dollar spectrum to AT&T. These transactions relieve EchoStar's financial pressure and give it a potentially huge stake in Elon Musk's SpaceX.

MarketWatch reported that JPMorgan believes investors are valuing EchoStar at roughly a 40% discount to its estimated net asset value, or what its investments and remaining businesses may be worth after accounting for liabilities.

EchoStar may seem less like a satellite firm and more like an indirect, perhaps discounted, method to own Musk's space company to investors who believe SpaceX has more capacity to grow.

JPMorgan says EchoStar has become a different company

Spectrum is where EchoStar's transition begins.

In July, the company completed the sale of its 3.45 gigahertz and 600 megahertz licenses to AT&T. EchoStar received $20.25 billion in cash, while AT&T deposited another $2.4 billion into a federally mandated creditor trust, according to an EchoStar filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

For stockholders, the SpaceX deal may be even more significant.

EchoStar's revised agreement values wireless spectrum at $20 billion. Up to $11 billion in SpaceX shares may be paid to settle EchoStar's spectrum debt.

According to EchoStar's second-quarter filing, the company now targets the final spectrum acquisition closing for around Nov. 30, 2027.

That is a significant shift from EchoStar's previous position.

Before these deals, the company was confronting large debt obligations and regulatory pressure over spectrum that the Federal Communications Commission believed was being underused. EchoStar said in its filing that regulators had raised the possibility of license revocations unless the company sold a meaningful portion of those assets.

JPMorgan believes the sales eliminate the balance-sheet problem and leave shareholders with assets whose value may not yet be reflected in EchoStar's stock price.

JPMorgan called the valuation discount "unwarranted."

Better Dividend Stock for Retirees: AT&T vs. Comcast ©kittichai boonpong's Images and Anderson Wei from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

AT&T yields 4.6% and plans to hold its dividend at $1.11 a share, while Comcast yields 6.5% after raising its dividend 7.5% a year from fiscal 2020 to fiscal 2025.

Over the twelve months to June 30, 2026, AT&T's dividend took 45% of its free cash flow, and Comcast's took 24%.

Analysts expect Comcast's free cash flow to fall in fiscal 2026, which would raise its dividend to 36% of free cash flow, against 46% at AT&T.

Comcast plans to separate NBCUniversal and Sky in a spin-off within about a year and hasn't yet set a dividend policy for the two companies.

Retirees living off their portfolios want a dividend check they can count on, and two of the biggest names in connectivity are offering very different checks right now.

AT&T (T:NYSE) yields 4.6% and plans to hold its dividend at $1.11 a share while returning $45 billion+ to shareholders from 2026 to 2028. Comcast (CMCSA:NASDAQ) pays more, at 6.5%. But it plans to separate NBCUniversal and Sky in a spin-off within about a year, and it hasn't said what its dividend will look like after that.

So which is the better dividend stock for retirees?

AT&T: a steady $1.11, with room to spare

AT&T's dividend fell from $2.08 a share in fiscal 2020 to $1.11 in fiscal 2025, and management plans to keep it there. At that level it's well-covered. It took 45% of free cash flow over the twelve months to June 30, 2026, and it takes 46% on analysts' fiscal 2026 consensus. In each fiscal year from 2023 to 2025, it took between 40% and 44% of free cash flow.

AT&T (T): free cash flow vs. dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2016–2025 (TIKR)

The business behind the dividend is growing. Second-quarter 2026 revenue rose 2.3% from a year earlier to $31.6 billion, and service revenue from fiber and wireless rose 5.1% as AT&T retires its copper network. As CEO John Stankey put it, "where we have fiber, we win with fiber and wireless."

Management expects free cash flow of $18 billion+ in 2026, rising to $21 billion+ in 2028. It plans to spend essentially all of this year's free cash flow on dividends and buybacks. The main risk is debt. Net debt is 2.91x EBITDA over the last twelve months, and AT&T expects that ratio to rise after its EchoStar deal closes. It then expects to return to its 2.5x target range within about three years.

Comcast: a bigger check, with a breakup ahead

Comcast's dividend has gone the other way, rising from $0.92 a share in fiscal 2020 to $1.32 in fiscal 2025, or 7.5% a year. By TIKR's figures, it has gone up every fiscal year for 17 years through fiscal 2025. It also took a slim 24% of free cash flow over the twelve months to June 30, 2026.

Key Takeaways

AT&T plans to keep its dividend at $1.11 a share a year while it speeds up buybacks to about $10 billion in 2026.

Altria yields 6.5% to AT&T's 4.6%, and its dividend per share grew 4% a year from fiscal 2020 to fiscal 2025.

AT&T's dividend took 45% of its free cash flow over the twelve months to June 2026, against 78% at Altria.

Altria carries less than half AT&T's leverage, and AT&T expects its leverage to rise after its EchoStar deal closes.

If you own AT&T (T:NYSE) for the dividend, don't wait on a raise. With its second-quarter results on July 22, AT&T said it plans to keep its dividend at $1.11 a share a year while it speeds up share repurchases to about $10 billion in 2026.

Altria Group (MO:NYSE), which reported on July 30, has kept raising instead. Its dividend per share grew 4.1% a year from fiscal 2020 to fiscal 2025, and it yields 6.5% to AT&T's 4.6%.

So which is the better dividend stock?

AT&T has room to spare, and it's buying back stock

AT&T's Advanced Connectivity service revenue, from fiber and wireless, rose 5.1% from a year earlier to $23.5 billion in the second quarter of 2026.

That growth leaves the dividend well-covered, at 45% of free cash flow over the twelve months to June 30, 2026. Dividends paid fell from $15.1 billion in fiscal 2021 to $8.14 billion in fiscal 2023, and free cash flow has run more than twice that every year since.

AT&T (T): free cash flow vs. dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2016–2025 (TIKR)

So where does the spare cash go? On the second-quarter call, management put it plainly: "Together, our planned share repurchases and expected dividend payments will total approximately $18 billion this year, which is essentially 100% of our outlook for free cash flow."

Debt is the main risk. TIKR puts AT&T's net debt at 2.91x EBITDA over the last twelve months. The company expects its own leverage measure to rise after its EchoStar deal closes, then return to its 2.5x target range within about three years.

Altria spends most of its cash on the dividend

Where AT&T keeps a wide cushion, Altria runs much closer to the line. Its domestic cigarette shipment volumes are falling, while on! PLUS nicotine pouches, expanded to 120,000 stores, are doing the growing. Even so, adjusted diluted EPS rose 4.9% to $2.80 in the first half of 2026 from a year earlier, and Altria guides to $5.61 to $5.72 for 2026.

Its dividend took 78% of free cash flow over the twelve months to June 30, 2026. That's high, but steady: the ratio stayed between 74.6% and 82.0% every fiscal year from 2021 to 2025. Free cash flow climbed from $3.64 billion in fiscal 2016 to $9.07 billion in fiscal 2025, and it has topped dividends paid every year since fiscal 2018.

title: Service Guarantees And League Deals Could Change The Case For AT&T Stock

Service Guarantees And League Deals Could Change The Case For AT&T Stock
Sasha Jovanovic

Trading disclosure

AT&T recently outlined several moves across its core business, including expanded customer guarantees, a new NBA and WNBA High-Speed Arena Network, a fiber joint venture agreement, and the planned retirement of long-serving executive Lori M. Lee at the end of 2026.

The broadened AT&T Guarantee and deeper partnerships with leagues and utilities highlight a push to tie premium connectivity, service reliability, and bundled offers more tightly to recurring customer relationships.

We will look at how AT&T's investment narrative interacts with the expanded AT&T Guarantee and what that could signal.

Position your portfolio for the same fiber-and-connectivity theme driving AT&T by scanning a curated 55 AI infrastructure stocks that could benefit from similar long-term demand.

AT&T Investment Narrative Recap

To own AT&T, you need to believe the heavy lift into fiber, 5G and converged bundles can keep recurring service revenue resilient even as legacy copper assets and heavy debt remain a drag. The key near term swing factor remains execution on fiber rollout and cost takeout, which these announcements do not fundamentally change.

The biggest risk still sits in margins and cash flow if equipment subsidies stay rich while earnings are forecast to decline 1.5% a year over the next three years. Customer friendly offers such as aggressive trade ins and richer guarantees add pressure if they are not matched by higher account value and lower churn.

The expanded AT&T Guarantee is the clearest operational link to near term catalysts. Faster call response, AI generated care recaps and outage credits all push toward a cleaner service reputation and, if delivered consistently, can support the thesis that converged fiber and wireless customers are stickier and more valuable.

There is a trade off. These commitments raise the bar on execution and may increase short term service and support costs. For an investor watching whether service revenue and bundled penetration offset device subsidies and copper exit costs, the critical question is whether this guarantee framework tightens loyalty enough to support that convergence narrative.

What The AT&T Forecasts Are Actually Pricing In

Analysts are effectively asking you to underwrite an AT&T story where fiber and connectivity keep revenue creeping higher while earnings step down over time. Revenue is modeled to rise by 2.5% a year over the next few years, yet profit margins are expected to compress from 16.9% today to 13.7% in 3 years. That mix suggests a bigger top line carrying less profit per dollar, which raises the bar for execution on all the service and support promises wrapped into the new AT&T Guarantee.

detail:

Telecom Analyst Slams Verizon vs SpaceX: "What Is Verizon's Differentiation? They Have None" ©metamorworks from Getty Images Pro and tatyanakorenyugina via Canva
Key Takeaways

SpaceX agreed on Oct. 8 to buy Grain Management's 800 MHz spectrum for a reported $8 billion, and Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile US each fell more than 10% the next day.

LightShed Partners analyst Walter Piecyk says Verizon has nothing left to set it apart, and the numbers back him up.

Verizon's revenue grew only from $134 billion in fiscal 2021 to $138 billion in fiscal 2025, while its total debt reached $185 billion.

SpaceX expects upgraded Starlink Mobile service by the end of 2027, and Verizon reports third-quarter results on Oct. 26.

SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) is coming for the wireless carriers, and one longtime telecom analyst thinks he knows which one is in the most trouble: Verizon (VZ:NYSE).

On Oct. 8, SpaceX agreed to buy Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz spectrum for Starlink Mobile. The Wall Street Journal valued the deal at around $8 billion. Verizon, AT&T (T:NYSE), and T-Mobile US (TMUS:NASDAQ) each fell more than 10% the next day.

On the latest episode of Decoder, host Nilay Patel asked LightShed Partners analyst Walter Piecyk why Verizon has the most to lose. His answer:

"What is Verizon's differentiation in the market right now? They have none."

Ouch.

A 60% margin on a commodity

Piecyk starts with the network, which used to be Verizon's whole pitch. For years it sold itself as the best network, and he says T-Mobile has taken that title. When Patel asked whether it's gone for good, Piecyk didn't hedge: "I think that's completely gone."

That leaves an industry earning big margins on what he sees as the same product everywhere:

"The networks are effectively commoditized. These networks are basically the same, right? And they're getting 60% margins."

Verizon's own EBITDA margin sits below Piecyk's 60%, but look at how little it moves: between 35% and 36% every year from fiscal 2022 to fiscal 2025. A margin that steady, on a product Piecyk calls a commodity, is exactly what draws a new entrant in…

Verizon EBITDA Margin (TIKR)

Layoffs under Verizon's new CEO can prop that margin up for now, and Piecyk gives them that much. The cuts "may appease investors to make the EBITDA look good for the next couple of quarters, but at some point you have to show and have a strategy for some type of revenue growth."

Where's the growth?

That's the bigger problem. Piecyk laid out how SpaceX bulls could build their case from here: Starlink Mobile wins its first 5 million or 10 million customers, and then "Verizon is going to be so desperate for any type of revenue because their revenue declined. They're just going to hand them a wholesale deal and then they'll start selling spectrum."
